messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 44
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Nurse
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Mirror Checking: keep checking mirrors, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Hopelessness: I have no future

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kiet Phommasack is a 44-year-old Lao-American man who has worked as a registered nurse in a busy urban hospital for nearly fifteen years. He is married, the father of two teenage children, and until approximately eight months ago was regarded by colleagues as one of the steadiest, most dependable members of his unit. He presents now with a PCL-5 score of 68, seeking help for the first time after his wife told him, quietly but firmly, that she no longer recognised the man she had married.

The event that brought Kiet to this point occurred on a Tuesday evening in late autumn. He had finished a twelve-hour shift and was walking the four blocks to the parking garage, still in his scrubs, when two men approached him from a recessed doorway. One pressed what Kiet felt as a hard, blunt object into his lower back while the other struck him across the left side of his face and shoved him against a brick wall. They took his wallet, his phone, and the bag he was carrying. The blow to his face split his cheekbone. Before they ran, one of them struck him again in the ribs. Kiet did not lose consciousness, but he remained against the wall for several minutes, unable to move, listening to his own breathing and the receding sound of footsteps.

In the weeks that followed, the memory did not behave the way Kiet expected a memory to behave. It did not soften or blur. Instead it returned in discrete, frozen images — the texture of the brick against his palm, the specific angle of the streetlight above the doorway, the dark fabric of a jacket sleeve — each image arriving with the same flat, absolute clarity as a photograph pulled from a sleeve. When these images surfaced, the pain in his cheekbone and ribs returned with them, a physical echo that he could not explain and that frightened him considerably. He had come to believe that his body was somehow still there, still against that wall, and that some part of him had never entirely left.

What frightened him most, beyond the pain, was the conclusion he found himself returning to in quiet moments: that there was something about him that had invited what happened. He had been wearing scrubs. He had been walking alone. He had not been alert enough. He was certain, in a way he could not argue himself out of, that a different kind of man — a more careful, more capable man — would have seen it coming. This belief had calcified into something broader and darker: that nothing good could come to him now, that the future he had been quietly building had been foreclosed. He did not say these things aloud to his wife, but they shaped nearly every hour of his waking life.

At work, the consequences became concrete and cumulative. The hospital parking garage was four blocks away, and Kiet began arriving an hour early each shift so he could park directly outside the building, even when no spaces were available and he received citations for it. On the unit, he chose his break-room seat only after scanning which chair offered a clear view of both doors. He checked the corridor mirrors at the nurses' station repeatedly throughout each shift — the convex safety mirrors installed at hallway junctions — pausing at each one longer than any clinical task required. He looked behind him when he walked between wards. Colleagues noticed. A charge nurse asked, gently, whether he was all right. Kiet said he was tired.

At home, sleep came reluctantly and left early. He kept the television on through the night, not to watch it but to keep his mind moving, occupied, away from the stillness in which the images returned most forcefully. His wife described lying beside him while he stared at the ceiling, present in body but somewhere she could not reach.

It was she who finally named what she saw — not with clinical language but with a grief that cut through his resistance. Kiet made the appointment the following morning. He arrives hoping, in some tentative and half-disbelieved way, that he might be told the future is not as sealed as it feels. What he fears most is being told, in some form or another, that he is right.
